body:
In article <199706081420211480229@remote4-line36.cis.yale.edu>,
Peter Bell <bell@pantheon.yale.edu> wrote:
>
> categorize his parents as True Believers) and people in academic
> circles.  There's a certain formalism to the construction of the
> manifesto that seems like some sort of an attempt at a nod to
> academics.

Well, he does say in his manifesto that he intends to convince the
academics first, and leave the conversion of the masses until later.
He seems to approach it like a marxist might: convince the
discontented amoung the middle or upper class, and let them convince
the lower class.  However, I don't see that this approach would
necessarily work in America.

>> It the manifesto had been more articulate and convincing, I believe
>> he would have generated tenfold more interest in his beliefs.
>
> I'm actually not sure that I agree; you're assuming people would
> have read it.  Americans, his chosen group, simply do not read.

Look at the nonfiction on the New York Times bestseller list. :) We
*do* read, just not things like Aristotle or Thomas Aquiness. As to
the literary types, I'm not so sure you are correct there. Of course,
I could imagine that it is true since there is so *much* material out
there, for each field, that it must be impossible to keep fully up to
date.

I'm interested in this subject myself.  How different would society be
if we all were brought up to believe that a broad education and the
desire to learn and develop our minds was an essential component of
life? 


> [television] can be used to convince Americans of *anything,* if
> used properly.

Humph, you mean like presidential elections? :)

>> I certainly wouldn't have taken any notice of his
>> manifesto he had gone about getting it published in a normal way.
>
> Do you think you might have run across similar strains of thought
> later on in your life? 

I had run across stuff, but I never paid any attention to it.  My area
in college was political science, so I did look at some things
regarding the effects of technology on society, but never modern
technology in the here and now.

>      Section 1.  Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a
>      punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly
>      convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place
>      subject to their jurisdiction.  
>
> Prisoners are now being employed to make a popular line of blue
> jeans in Oregon, to take reservations by a number of hotel chains,
> and for an ever-growing variety of tasks as more and more states see
> self-sufficiency for prisons by hiring out the inmates as a
> necessity.

Other then "human rights" abuses, there is the whole question of
politcal prisoners who are being "reeducated through labor."  I don't
think there is a valid comparison between China and the US. the US, in
general, isn't in the habit of picking up every political dissenter
and throwing him in prison until his will is broken.  This isn't to
say that individuals aren't above doing that (as you seem to know very
well, we only have to look at the civil rights movements for
examples), but that it isn't a recognized national policy.


> The problem I have with terrorists/freedom fighters/revolutions/wars
> as a whole is this: assume one side just, and one is not.  The side
> which is in the wrong is there because of policy which has been
> authored by its leaders.  Rarely are the killers for justice in a
> position to kill the authors of injustice; rather, they are killing
> others who are acting lawfully.  So, in the best possible case we
> have just warriors and lawful warriors killing one another.  Not
> just warriors and the authors of the unjust laws.  And it's very,
> very rarely close to that clean-cut.

Well, I sort of agree with this.  It isn't clear cut, but don't you
think that this is the easy way out?  To essentially say that, since
they operated within a legal framework, they can't be punished?  Say
you have people who have been picked up off the street and tortured.
A year later, a new government is in place. These people see their
torturers walking around free as a bird. There is likely to be a lot
of anger in that society...

But in any case, my point essentially matches with yours.  I'm not
sure if you saw that I was being very sarcastic when I wrote:

  acceptable as long as they don't turn around and start slaughtering
  everyone from the other group when they get the chance (which slims
  the group down a touch).


>> One example is the Vietnam conflict.  Lots of people say that the
>> North Vietnamese were liberating their fellows from the capitalist
>> pigs.
>
> Wow, where do you hang out?  I haven't heard this argument in years, and
> rarely heard it even in Berkeley during the 80's.  

You are very lucky. I heard it all the time for a whole semester when
I took a class that examined the 60s and 70s in America.  Thena gain,
my college was weird: freshmen are usually 15 or 16 years old.  Since
this was a junior level class, my classmates were around 18 years old.
Perhaps they didn't have a very broad perspective on the matter. :) In
any case, that crap is what I had to argue against all the time.

But, back to my point: I wasn't writing about the cause of the war,
but was making the argument that there were people who couldn't give a
damn about which side wanted what government, as long as they were
left in peace.  Some hated Diem's government, others hated the Viet
Minh, probably many hated both.


> I'd be interested in asking whether that soldier knew there'd been
> elections which the nationalists won in the mid-50's.  Not many
> folks do; I didn't learn about until 1989 or so, as for some odd
> reason, it's not mentioned much by the media.  Also, what I've read

This isn't what I've read. From what I'd heard, the elections never
occurred in the South.  Not to say that the south wouldn't have voted
nationalist, Diem was doing a wonderful job of pissing off almost
everyone...

From what I've read:

Japan essentially took control of Vietnam over from France (who were
under German control at this point) during World War II.  At that time
the Viet Minh was organized from the nationalist movements that had
sprung up because of massive discontent during French rule
("protection" is what the French called it). The nationalists were
prepared to seize power when Japan was defeated by America.  The Viet
Minh took over North Vietnam, and also invaded South Vietnam (there
has already been a North and South for a long, long time).  The French
fought them, drove them out of the South, and both parties tried to
negotiate a settlement.  This attempt failed, and war broke out.

The French had US aid, and were powerful enough to to force the Viet
Minh into adopting guerrilla warfare tactics.  Dien Bien Phu was a
turning point, and France finally agreed to negotiations.  This was in
1954.  Both sides were to have elections in 1956. Diem came into power
in the South, and never held elections.

So where did you read about elections being held in the South?


>> It is simply this: to admire a group fighting for its principles is
>> never black and white.  The wrongs and rights of both sides can be
>> examined and found to contain "truth."
>
> I'd be interested in your comments on Ghandi's wrongs and on the
> wrongs committed by the Southern Christian Leadership Council in
> Mississippi.

You over-interpreted me here.  The context was two groups who are
being physically unpleasant to each other (that is, both sides are
violent).


>> Were the Unabomber victims evil people who were destroying the
>> world? [Not really. Were they part of the system that could be seen
>> as destroying the world? Yes. Does that make it right to kill them?
>> Nope, nor does it come across as a valiant freedom fighter's
>> methods.]
>
> How much sympathy do you have for the fellow who was a lead lobbyist
> for the timber industry?  If he'd been a lead lobbyist for the
> tobacco industry?  I ask, because my reading of the coverage is that
> a lot more emphasis is being put on the advertising executive who
> was both apparently wrongly targeted and at more of a remove from
> the industry in question even had he been rightly targeted, and on
> the "harmless academic" victims than on the timber lobbyist.

Why did you just quote the first sentence of my paragraph?  To answer
your question, I have a lot of sympathy for *all* the victims and the
family and friends of those victims. I don't think it was justifiable
to make *any* of those attacks.  Why in the world would I feel it was
more justifiable to kill a lobbyist as opposed to a scientist?
Neither one, as far as I know, were sitting around plotting world
domination and the destruction of all things green.

As to what the media puts out, I can't answer for them.  Perhaps they
see this as a Greenpeace movement, and aren't looking any further then
that.


>> I'm just making the point that killing people for a "righteous
>> cause" doesn't mean we can or should hold hold a terrorist up for
>> admiration.
>
> [List of people/companies who have been involved with death and not
> condemned as criminal madmen removed]
>
> Terrorists in suits, and all of them far more lethal and far less
> selective than F.C.  While you may or may not agree with FC's target
> selection, the bombs were not indiscriminate, which puts them a rung
> ahead on people who are insulated by complicated command structures
> from their actions.

I can only assume that you are trying to make the point that, if
society looks the other way when the US goes to war with someone, they
are hypocrites for thinking that the Unabomber is a criminal.  Well,
welcome to the world of nations, national policy, and the law. The
world certainly isn't a fair place, you get no argument from me
there. Strength seems to do a lot more then make "right" -- it also
seems to make morals for most of society. Sad, but true.

Hmm, let me see... Ah, here in the manifesto I find the following:

   135. In paragraph 125 we used an analogy of a weak neighbor who is
   left destitute by a strong neighbor who takes all his land by forcing
   on him a series of compromises. But suppose now that the strong
   neighbor gets sick, so that he is unable to defend himself. The weak
   neighbor can force the strong one to give him his land back, or he can
   kill him. If he lets the strong man survive and only forces him to
   give his land back, he is a fool, because when the strong man gets
   well he will again take all the land for himself. The only sensible
   alternative for the weaker man is to kill the strong one while he has
   the chance. [...]

By his own logic, the stronger neighbor should kill the weaker one
before any chance for retaliation occurs.  I think the Unabomber is
trapped in his own logic here.  If TK is the Unabomber, how many
people here think he will be sentenced to death?

>> Well, the only thing I can say is that you need to examine why it is
>> that you need an immediate, live, "hero figure" in order to feel that
>> there is a reason to see worthiness (empowerment) in your beliefs.
>> (Dr. Spock: "So, tell me about your childhood.")
>
> I don't think this is fair.  Criticizing people for wanting heroic
> figures is like criticizing people for breathing.  On the other hand,
> there are people who are heroic figures in my mind who've come to my
> attention only because of what they've written.  Camus would be one.
> For many, Marx would be another - and in both cases, really, all either
> of them did was write.  

I think it is perfectly fair. I'm not criticizing her for wanting one,
but for needing one to feel "psychologically empower[ed]" about her
beliefs.  Personally, the trite phrase "I believe in what I believe."
sums it up.  I have reasons to back up most of those beliefs (and am
working on the others...), but I don't see how meeting someone who
agrees with me should make me feel so much better about my beliefs.

> Absolutely.  An alternate path would - and hopefully will - work
> better.  I think though, that there is an inconsistency inherent to
> our society about when we will and will not kill, and a desperate
> eagerness to be blinded by what our leaders tell us about why
> they've made the decisions they've made.

I can't see applying the term "consistent" to a society.  It is like
saying you can rationalize with a mob.  What makes you think that the
majority of Americans are immune from feeling the urge to either
dominate or to feel like they are doing a good deed?

For example, I believe many people got a kick out of the Gulf War:
seeing US troops in successful action, and seeing themselves as a
nation helping Kuwait. I don't think they were "eager to be blinded"
into believing this, I think they already believed it.  National
policy is expressed by what the people want. The seed is there, the PR
people just take advantage of it.

> Does Kennan -- and his list of unreal ojectives -- read to anyone
> else as applying more broadly than to foreign policy?  Whether it
> does or doesn't, what does it say about any moral authority our
> government has to take life in war?  If it does apply at home, as it
> seems to me it must, what does it say about the authority our
> government has to take life under any circumstances?

The moral authority for our government to take life comes from the
democratic majority of course. Each member of the majority of society
is willing to give the government certain powers and authorities in
order in ensure a relatively pleasant life for himself or herself.  If
the society becomes too large, government becomes unwieldy. It is
unable to give the people a sense of control over their lives.  People
become apathetic about their ability to make a difference.  The
political powers become an entity unto itself. Politicians grab for
votes by saying "yes" to all the concerns voters have. The population
begins to think it is too much trouble to get up and vote because "it
is all the same anyway." And on and on and on...

Sad, isn't it?
